Vice Chancellors in a Vice Grip

By: Liz Fish | Production

Proposal


Show:

Summary:
Will vice chancellors become the next victims of campus chaos? The country is reeling in the wake of ongoing violence, vandalism and racial dissent on varsity campuses that have jeopardised the academic year ahead and seen legitimate student movements hijacked to further political agendas. University of Cape Town’s Max Price and Wits University’s Adam Habib provide Carte Blanche with unique and critical insight into the enormous pressure faced by leaders of tertiary institutions.


Further information:
Has the Fees Must Fall movement been hijacked by political parties? The start of the academic year has been disrupted on campuses across the country. At UCT, Vice Chancellor Max Price’s office was burnt out, residences raided and paintings burnt, buildings re-named. Students have laid charges of violence against Dr Price. At Free State and Pretoria Universities there have been running battles between students with EFF supporters coming onto campus. At Wits University buses have been burnt. SRC's have distanced hemselves from radical action on campus- the student and academic bodies are divided. At all the Universities the Vice Chancellors are being called on to resign.
What impact is this having on the academic year? What is the way forward and are outside political agendas being played out on campuses, hijacking the academic programme and putting universities in jeopardy.
In-depth interviews with Dr Max Price and Prof Adam Habib will explore the the challenges Vice Chancellors are facing trying to hold the academic institutions on track with outside political agendas playing themselves out.

Press Release:


Vice Chancellors in a Vice Grip
Will vice chancellors become the next victims of campus chaos? The country is reeling in the wake of ongoing violence, vandalism and racial dissent on varsity campuses that have jeopardised the academic year ahead and seen legitimate student movements hijacked to further political agendas. University of Cape Town’s Max Price and Wits University’s Adam Habib provide unique and critical insight into the enormous pressure faced by leaders of tertiary institutions.


Script:


Script: University Vice-Chancellors across the country have endured the most stressful six months of their careers, finding themselves on the other side of the barricades in a crisis they had been predicting for years. What started out as a largely peaceful mass student uprising has increasingly turned violent. WITS Universities Professor Adam Habib, chairs The Board of Universities South Africa.
Habib “I found myself in an existential crisis I always thought I would be on the opposite side of the barricade little did I think I would have to manage the barricades
Script: Despite having his office petrol bombed, UCT’s Dr Max Price Vice remains optimistic
Price “Not to say that I am not terribly stressed I am, and that I don’t worry every day about what’s going to happen but I certainly think we are on track to come through this, remain a good university, a strong university, more transformed and a new identity actually and an identity that is more African
Script: It all began at Wits last October
Habib” The students achieved in 7 days what Vice- Chancellors had been talking about for 10 years and it demonstrated the power of social movements…. The systemic parameters opened in ways that would never have opened with polite conversation of the Vice-Chancellors social action did that
Bongani “One of the thinks that was striking things about fees must fall that it seemed to bring people across racial lines, across class divides you know it had no political agenda
Habib “It was an expression of a nation saying this no longer can continue. And when you saw those students marching on parliament, when you saw young white kids and young black kids rich kids and poor kids saying, fees cannot go up like they are denying poor people access to higher education I think it was the most glorious moment of this nation.
Bongani: “ So what changed in 2016?
Habib “On the first day of the registration process there was a small group of students who said to us they were not going to allow registration to happen. They effectively said if there is no free education there is no education at all despite the multiple concessions.
Price “The threat to the future to higher education I think primarily is a threat around funding and hasn’t been addressed in the long term. The current protests because there is at least a core group in the protest movement that wants to disrupt Universities disrupt the government and their goal is not the goal of funding or accommodation or insourcing or decolonization or transformation that group has a view that SA has never gone through the kinds of change that are needed
Script: This group argues for a violent overthrow of the status quo, consequently over the last few weeks the atmosphere on campuses across the country has become chaotic. A bus at WITS burnt with students inside, portraits set alight, poo in lecture theatres at UCT , racial violence at the University of the Free State and the most extreme - the burning of several buildings at the North West University.
Habib “It seems to me that there are three lessons have been lost from the October protests. The first of the October protest was that it was cross party cross class cross race and what we have seen increasingly is racist expressions by a small groups of people What you have now seen is violence and frankly we have to draw the a line in the sand…. ….There has been a glorification of violence. …..and I think they need to be challenged around this.
Price “The graffiti and the T-shirts which say fuck whites or kill all whites these are is what I consider racist or hostility towards not just whites but also coloureds and Indians… and that group is determined to pursue violence
John “Does that worry you Dr Price where you have to deal with a group where anarchy is a necessary part of the process
Price “Absolutely it does because a small group can never the less cause widespread disruption and it just changes the mood on the campus there is a tension there is an anxiety that something will happen and you don’t know when and what it requires us to have much more security and that is expensive because you don’t know what is going to happen.
John “Its fallen to University Administration to negotiate with the protesting students their complaints have varied from outsourcing to language and accommodation but alarmingly there appears to be a growing reluctance to negotiate and compromise
Habib “I think there are shifting demands and there is what I call a lack of thoughtful activism a lack of pragmatism a lack of understanding that to address challenges require compromise it requires thoughtful engagement it requires hard trade-offs it requires political will and choices to be made
Bongani “Language and race remain central pillars of these protests
Habib “Yes to addressing race yes to addressing language but that does not mean you must forsake the commitment to building a non-racial identity and to building a more egalitarian society
Price: “This umbrella group has a mode of politics which rejects structure and bureaucracy and therefore rejects the idea that there should be people who are elected as leaders who could easily be held accountable to the group- the people who one negotiates with can change from time to time you believe you are making progress on one issue and when it goes back to a plenary or something it changes. The difference between the recognised structures such as the SRC and other groups that feel either that the SRC doesn’t represent them or for political reasons is hostile to the SRC. On many other campuses it has turned into a party political battle and the challenge for a Vice-Chancellor is do you ignore those other structures because they are not represented they are not accountable, and you ignore the other lobbies at your peril
Bongani: Has Minister Mzimande shown adequate leadership on this?
Habib “I think he is trying. But it has to involve the Ministry, but it requires the treasury it requires the Vice-Chancellors it requires the students and you know I want to hear other stakeholders. I want to see parents stand up and say look I don’t think it is appropriate for students to be burning places down I think it is important for the unions to be say I don’t think you should be burning things down. That this can’t be an issue for Vice-Chancellors, you know security isn’t going to resolve this questions security will protect us for a while but is the collective of society that has to say our institutions are important and we need a thoughtful engagement and no burning to happen
John “The consequences for academia are severe, you are talking about short term political gain at any, at any cost
Price“ My plea to political leaders and anyone out there is to understand how long it takes to build up a higher education system, and SA has a really good higher education system, globally competitive, producing research that competes, producing professionals. And we are on a knife edge. I think if universities were to shut for a year or for a few months not only would there be a cohort of school leavers who are delayed and maybe deprived of that education but we would lose tons of staff we would lose the ability to attract international students and staff which substantially improves what we do and our reputation and our ability to partner with universities globally
Habib ‘My worry about the universities is if we lose these Universities the one higher education system that works on the African continent will be destroyed. If we lose these institutions we will reinforce the very inequality we are fighting about
Link: The countries Vice-Chancellors are increasingly coming under personal attack with some protesting students saying that they are a part of the problem this was illustrated starkly with the torching of Max Prices office
Price “I see this as part of the attack of the authority of the University on the legitimacy of the authority structures
John: Do you think that the Vice-Chancellors because they are the faces of the various Universities are bearing the brunt of all this?
Price “They are certainly bearing the brunt I think it’s going to be very hard to fill the vacancies right now, there are not a lot of people lining up for the job because of the stresses and because of the challenges and the attacks are often very personalised. .I think it is unfair when ones integrity is questioned when ones values are questioned. Many of the Vice-Chancellors have sort of struggle credentials, and to suggest that just because they are now vice- chancellors their value systems have changed I think it’s wrong
Bongani “Are you on some level disappointed, hurt maybe?
Habib “Obviously there are times that I go through and existential crisis when people say to me you have sold out I believe that what I am doing is trying in this context is understand the trade-offs and progressively move us to the socio- economic egalitarian future we are looking at
Bongani: “Even if it means being called Adolf Habib?
Habib “Even if it’ means been called Adolf Habib. What you need to do is play the cards you are dealt in as best a way you can towards the egalitarian future you want and to do so with a clear conscious
John: “ So in spite of everything you remain optimistic?
Price: Ja absolutely
John “I am a little surprised
Price “We are going to emerge from this a stronger better university provided we can secure the funding which is somewhat out of our hands it’s a government issue and provided we can buffer the protests where it is necessary and accommodate the legitimate concerns
Bongani: ”Is this a defining moment of this generation of this time?
Habib “While we have achieved the political rights of 1994 the socio- economic rights have not been achieved and that is the agenda that we are engaging in, that defining struggle has begun.
